docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Verify your computer

You have read my getting started notes, and you know what sort of computer you need. But how do you verify if your home computer is suitable for this module and programme?

In our courses, desktop virtualization is done using VMware Workstation. This is education not training, however, I do audit and maintain some cross compatibility with industry certifications. I am going to assume you have basic competence with Windows.

There are other hypervisors, they will work for all activities.

For some e-delivery students, I am using Azure Labs and this will use Hyper-V only.

On campus, we use the University laboratories, you will use VMWare Workstation only.

When learning, we will use Windows GUI as always. However, all small data centre work is done using scripting; we figure out how to do something and then we write a script to do it. Whenever we do something in the GUI, we will also look at the script for doing the same task. When you are recording your work, you only record the scripts, not the GUI (no or few screenshots!).  

Over the years, there have been many changes in the way students carry out the practical exercises. As with all things in IT, the platforms we work with are characterized by change and instability; with each patch release, something that worked before no longer does. The exercises I demonstrate worked in the way I demonstrate, at a point in time, on the versions of code I show. You may need to adapt and figure out solutions where an example no longer works.

This is normal in our business, get used to it!

After reading those notes, you know what kind of computer you need and we will do all our exercises based on virtualization. There are some specific requirements before you can use your Windows 10/11 computer as a virtualization platform. The first thing we need to do is to understand what hardware is in the computer.

docs.title: Verifying the CPU
docs.text:
I can support Windows 10/11 or any edition of Windows Server 2016 or better. My practical exercises have not been tested on MAC OS and will probably not work on Apple hardware since the change to Mx processors.

There are some specific requirements before you can use your Windows 10/11 computer as a virtualization platform. The first thing we need to do is to understand what hardware is in the computer. We can verify most of what we need using systeminfo.exe from the command prompt.

In the example below, I’m running a Windows 11 Education instance on a home build PC.

Fig 1. SYSINFO on a VMWare PC.

Note that it tells me a hypervisor has been detected. This machine has VMWare Workstation installed.

Contrast that to one of my older Windows 10 machines, which has Hyper-V installed.

Fig 2. SYSINFO on a Huper-V PC.

In the previous screenshots I can see exactly the type of processor I have, the motherboard, and how much RAM I am using. At the end of this screenshot I can see the status of critical properties for virtualization. And they are all good! There are other things I can see that are mandatory for virtualization;

  • A 64-bit version of Windows.
  • The professional or education version.
  • Enough main memory (32GB).

docs.title: Secondary Storage
docs.text:
I also need to map the available disks and see if I have suitable secondary storage for virtual machines. If I run diskpart.exe and then type the command list disk, I can get an idea of what disks are in my system.

Fig 3. List disk.

I need to determine which disks are spinning disks (HDD) and which are solid-state (SSD). A quick way to do this is to run dfrgui.exe, the defragmentation tool. I can clearly see the drive types in my system.

Fig 4. Output from dfrgui.

This configuration is actually pretty good;

  • C: is a small SSD specifically intended for the host operating system.
  • I have a dedicated disk E: for synchronizing my cloud shares
  • A separate dedicated disk F: for holding static information, like ISO files.
  • Finally, I have a dedicated SSD G: for VM’s.

If I was running a lot of VM’s, I could improve the performance by adding more, small SSD’s.

docs.title: Finally
docs.text:
You know what to look for and you know what you need.

Verify if your home PC is suitable for virtualization now.
